figures.title: The table is a lookup, not an ordering
figures.caption: Four rows of the chapter's two-dimensional toy table. The token id selects a row by offset; the row's coordinates are the vector the rest of the network reads. The id is a merge-order position, so adjacent rows are not semantically adjacent, and nothing in the number says man is near woman.
figures.alt: A table with four rows and two columns, labelled d0 and d1. Row 0 is (1.0, 0.2), row 1 is (0.9, 0.7), row 2 is (0.8, 0.1), row 3 is (0.7, 0.6). Row 2 is highlighted as the row an id selects. The left-hand row numbers are positions in this excerpt, not token ids with any order.

data.row_head: V rows, one per vocabulary id
data.note: The highlighted row is the one the id selects. The row numbers are positions in this excerpt, not a rank: the id records when a BPE merge happened. A gather returns one row; no arithmetic mixes rows.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to follow one lookup.

steps.label: A BPE id arrives as an integer.
The integer is an offset into E, which has V rows.
The gather returns exactly one row; no arithmetic mixes rows.
That row, of width d_model, becomes x in the residual stream.

figures.title: Same two rows, before and after the shared component comes out
figures.caption: The chapter's toy table scores two rows at cosine 0.917 before centering and 0.166 after the table mean is subtracted. The drop is the anisotropic cone coming out. The fix is All-but-the-Top: subtract the mean, then remove the top principal components.
figures.alt: Two panels. Left, raw rows: a is (1.6, 1.05) and b is (1.05, 1.6); their dot product is 3.36, each length is 1.914, and the cosine is 0.917. Right, after subtracting the mean m = (1, 1): a prime is (0.6, 0.05) and b prime is (0.05, 0.6); the dot product is 0.06, each length is 0.602, and the cosine is 0.166.

panels.title: raw rows, before centering
panels.note: Two unrelated rows already score 0.917. The table sits in a narrow cone, so a random pair is comfortably positive.

panels.title: after subtracting m = (1, 1)
panels.note: All-but-the-Top: subtract the mean, then remove each vector's projection onto the top principal components.

figures.title: Tying saves a second copy of the embedding matrix
figures.caption: Tying sets W = Eᵀ, so one V × d_model matrix serves both the input lookup and the output projection. GPT-2 small publishes 124M parameters with the matrix counted once; untied, the same model carries a second 38,597,376-number copy, about 163M, so tying saves roughly 24 percent of the untied count.
figures.alt: Three horizontal bars. The embedding matrix alone is 38,597,376 parameters. GPT-2 small with tied embeddings is 124M parameters. GPT-2 small untied is about 163M parameters, highlighted. The arithmetic 50,257 times 768 equals 38,597,376 is printed in the note.

data.note: 50,257 × 768 = 38,597,376. GPT-2's 124M already counts that matrix once. Untying adds a second copy: 124 + 38.6 ≈ 163M, so tying saves 38.6 / 163 ≈ 24% of the untied count. LLaMA-7B (32,000 × 4,096 = 131M) leaves the matrices untied.
